### Part 2 --- Evidence, models, and inference

The conceptual core. What a causal claim is, what the standard models estimate, where uncertainty comes from, the difference between explaining and predicting, and how inference goes wrong — taught on examples from industry and the news, before anyone opens a dataset. Teams form in the first meeting of this part, and it closes by writing the problem up and presenting it.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 2 | Sep 2 | **Causal language**<br><span class='goal'>Draw your own project's causal graph, say which variable you must condition on and which you must not touch, and leave with your team's ground rules agreed in writing.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Counterfactuals and potential outcomes; why every comparison is a claim about a world that did not happen. Causal graphs: confounders, colliders, mediators, back-door reasoning — and why controlling for everything makes things worse. Then the map for the rest of this half: every design we meet is a different way of closing a back door, and you will draw each one before you hear what it is called<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Teams are formed, and then each team writes down its own ground rules — while everybody still gets along, rather than negotiating it in November. Who does what. What happens when somebody misses a deadline. How you settle a disagreement, and when to bring it to me. One page, signed by everyone, handed in before you leave. The weekly check-in starts today | Your team's written ground rules — agreed and handed in today |
| 3 | Sep 9 | **Models and uncertainty**<br><span class='goal'>Read a coefficient in the units of the problem, say what a p-value does and does not tell you, and tell an explanatory question apart from a predictive one.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Linear regression, non-linear models, and count models — described, not derived: what each estimates and how to read a coefficient in the units of the problem. Then where uncertainty comes from: residuals and errors, sampling variation, what a standard error states, where p-values come from and what they are not. Finally the distinction that decides half the projects in this room — explaining versus predicting, and why a model that predicts well may tell you nothing about what to do<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Simulation lab: draw from a world you control. Watch the p-value distribution under the null, then change the sample size and the variation and watch it move. Then fit the same world in-sample and out-of-sample, and watch a model that looks excellent fail on data it has not seen. Nothing to install, no code to write | — |

False precision: dependence ignored, multiple testing, specification search<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Take a published claim apart: which failure is doing the damage, and would more data fix it? | — |
| 5 | Sep 23\* | **Controls and matching**<br><span class='goal'>Draw the back doors a set of controls closes, and state exactly what would have to be true for your regression coefficient to be read causally.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> We start where every design meeting from here starts — at the graph. Conditioning on observables, drawn: which back doors a set of controls closes, and the one you cannot see well enough to close. Then controls and matching in practice, and when a regression coefficient can be read causally. Why 'I added controls' is a claim about the graph rather than a technique, and exactly what would have to be true for it to hold<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Back to the graph you drew in meeting 2: could you close every back door with data you could actually obtain? Breakout rooms, then report back | — |
| 6 | Sep 30 | **Writing the problem**<br><span class='goal'>Reconstruct the outline behind somebody else's paper, build your own the same way — topic sentence by topic sentence — and defend your research problem in front of the room.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Academic writing I — the method. A paper is built outline first: one topic sentence per paragraph, in order, before any prose exists. We start backwards, taking a published paper apart into the outline that must have produced it — which is also this week's exercise, and the fastest way to see that good writing has a skeleton. Then forwards: outline, then sketch, then full text. Every written product in this course is submitted in those stages, so the argument is fixed before the sentences are. Then what a problem statement in particular has to do — scope, unit, population, and the 'so what' in the first sentence rather than the fourth paragraph — and the failure modes: the topic with no question, hedging, the buried claim, the review that reviews without arguing<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Each team presents its research problem to the room in five minutes and takes questions — the feedback you get here is what you write up this week. Then you rate your teammates for the first time | Present your research problem, in class · Rate your teammates |

### Part 3 --- Research designs

The ways applied economists get a credible estimate, from conditioning on observables to designs built on found variation — what variation each exploits, what each assumes, and how each fails.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 7 | Oct 7 | **Research designs I**<br><span class='goal'>Draw the graph for an experiment, an instrument, and a discontinuity, and say whether any of the three could work for your question.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Three designs, each drawn before it is described. Experiments: randomisation cuts every arrow into treatment, so there is no back door left to close. Instrumental variables: an arrow into treatment and none into the outcome except through it — the exclusion restriction is that missing arrow, which is why it cannot be tested. Regression discontinuity: nothing else jumps at the cutoff. For each: what variation it exploits, what it assumes, how it fails, and what it looks like done well<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Scenario clinic: given a question, draw the graph first and then say whether any of these three could work here — and if not, what you would need to have that you do not | Problem & literature — outline · Writing 1 — reverse outline |
| 8 | Oct 14 | **Research designs II**<br><span class='goal'>Draw your own project's design as a graph and name the single assumption carrying the estimate — the one you would have to defend to a sceptic.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> The same discipline on harder designs, each drawn first. Difference-in-differences: the confounders you cannot measure are the ones that do not move, and parallel trends is what that assumption looks like on the graph. Panel data with local fixed effects: which arrows the fixed effects erase, and which survive them untouched. Event studies: the same picture with time on it. For each, what identifying variation is left once the fixed effects are in, and what assumption is carrying the estimate<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Draw your own project's design and mark the assumption carrying it — the one you would have to defend to a sceptic. This is the figure that goes in your design paper's identification section, so draw it to keep | Problem & literature — sketch |

### Part 4 --- Measurement, data, and getting hold of it

The step most projects skip. Turning a construct into something a dataset can hold, working out what the design actually demands, and then the practical business of obtaining it — sources, proprietary access, data-use agreements, the IRB, and what scraping and APIs can and cannot get you.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 9 | Oct 21\* | **Measurement and data**<br><span class='goal'>Turn your central construct into a variable somebody could actually record, and specify the unit, frequency, span, and coverage your design demands.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Constructs and operationalization: how you turn 'sustainability', 'financial literacy', or 'market power' into a variable somebody could actually record, and what makes that measure defensible or indefensible. Validity, and what a proxy costs you. Then working backwards from the design to its data requirements: unit of observation, level of aggregation, time frequency, span, coverage, and which comparisons the data has to contain — can this be done with county-level data, or does it need individuals?<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> What to ask of a dataset before trusting anything it says: what is one row? how many are there? what is missing, and is it missing at random? what is the range, and are the extremes real? what changed over time, and did the definition change with it? Then the measurement clinic — the variable your question actually needs, and whether anything on earth measures it | Problem & literature — full, end of week · Writing 2 — reverse outline and repair |
| 10 | Oct 28 | **Getting the data**<br><span class='goal'>Name your data source, its access route, its timeline, and your plan B — and know whether you need IRB approval or a data-use agreement before January.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> The landscape: administrative records, official statistics, firm and platform data, purchased panels — what each costs in money and in months. Start with what Cornell already pays for: the library's licensed holdings and the Dewey marketplace through the Johnson College membership, met in meeting 1 and worked properly here. A surprising number of capstones propose buying data the College already subscribes to. Proprietary access and data-use agreements: who signs, how long it takes, and what they forbid you from publishing. Research ethics and the Cornell IRB: what needs approval, what does not, and how long it takes. Then scraping and APIs at awareness level — what they are, what they can and cannot get you, what the terms of service and the law actually say, and when paying for a licence is the cheaper answer. We do not write scrapers in this course; you need to know what to ask for and what it costs<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Academic writing II — the memo. Writing to a decision-maker rather than an examiner: the two-page discipline, the bottom line first, and the fallback that shows you thought about failure. Then the acquisition clinic: each team names its source, its access route, its timeline, and its plan B | Data feasibility memo — outline, in class |

Then the harder half — knowing whether the answer is right without reading the code. Row counts across a join, totals against a published figure, five raw records read by hand.
